name: Water cutting / dehydration

lead: Water cutting is the deliberate reduction of body water, through fluid restriction, sweating, sweatsuits and saunas, to look drier, leaner and more defined. It is borrowed from combat sports, where athletes cut to a lower weight class before weigh-ins, and is also referred to in bodybuilding for a dry look.

Because sweat is mostly water, weight lost this way is largely fluid, so the leaner look shows within hours and comes back with rehydration. The method is well documented in weigh-in sports, where sports medicine commentary describes it as dangerous.

paras: Methods described include restricting food and fluids, water-loading beforehand, exercise-induced sweating, sweatsuits and saunas, usually timed within days or hours of a weigh-in or photo. The effect is temporary and reverses once fluids are replaced.

Dehydration can cause headache, fatigue, confusion, seizures, heatstroke, hypernatremia and kidney problems. Losses of 15 to 25 percent of body water are described as fatal, and several weight-cutting athletes died in 2015, 2016 and 2017. Some organizations have changed their rules in response.

angle.text: Shedding body water through fluid restriction, sweating and saunas gives a visibly leaner, sharper look within hours, a method borrowed from combat-sports weight cuts. The result is temporary and the method carries documented dehydration risks, including deaths in weight-cutting athletes.

lead: Water cutting is the practice of rapidly reducing body water, usually to make a lower weight class in combat sports or rowing, and in some communities to appear leaner. Methods include restricting food and fluids, water-loading, sweating through exercise, sweatsuits and saunas.[1]

Dehydration is a deficit of total body water, with effects ranging from thirst and impaired cognition at 1 to 2 percent loss to deterioration at over 10 percent, and death at 15 to 25 percent.[2] Weight-cutting writing in the sources described acute water loss as very dangerous and generally advised against by nutrition experts.[1]
Documentation of the practice in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles is not covered in the sources reviewed here.
infobox: Rapid fluid loss before weigh-ins or events

paras: Weight cutting is described as having two forms: losing fat and muscle over weeks before an event, and losing water in the final days.[1] Some athletes diet and perform aerobic exercise instead, aiming to raise their strength-to-mass ratio.[1]

Dehydration signs include thirst, headache, nausea, reduced urine, confusion, and in severe cases seizures. Acute complications include hypovolemic shock, coma, heatstroke and hypernatremia, and rehydrating too quickly risks cerebral edema.[2] Dehydration also affects appearance, with sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes among listed findings.[2]

Reported deaths include Yang Jian Bing in December 2015, Jordan Coe in March 2016 and Jessica Lindsay in November 2017, all while cutting weight for fights.[1] ONE Championship subsequently banned dehydration-based cutting and moved to a 'walking weight' model with hydration testing.[1] A Perth physician urged regulators to adopt hydration tests, warning in 2018 that deaths were inevitable without regulation.[1] In another case, a fighter was suspended six months and fined after posting a video of himself vomiting while cutting.[1]

No studies found of deliberate water cutting for physique appearance. Studies of weight-cutting methods among professional MMA athletes and a 2013 IOC-related position statement on weight-sensitive sports are referenced in encyclopedic sources, although their findings are not detailed here.[1]

timeline.event: Yang Jian Bing dies of dehydration while cutting weight for a ONE Championship bout.[1]
Jordan Coe dies while cutting weight in Thailand.[1]
